details:
**The Old Man and the Sea**
Hemingway's 1952 novella and his most common giveaway. The aging Cuban fisherman Santiago, who has gone 84 days without catching a fish, hooks a giant marlin in the Gulf Stream and fights it for days, but sharks devour it on the way home, leaving only the skeleton. It won the Pulitzer Prize and helped win Hemingway the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**Santiago, Manolin, and "the great DiMaggio"**
Details from The Old Man and the Sea. Santiago is called "salao," the worst form of unlucky, so the boy Manolin is forced by his parents to fish on another boat. Santiago idolizes the baseball player Joe DiMaggio, talks to his cramped hand during the struggle, and repeatedly dreams of lions on an African beach.

**A Farewell to Arms**
Hemingway's 1929 World War I novel, drawn from his own service as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy. The American ambulance officer Frederic Henry, introduced by his friend the surgeon Rinaldi to the British nurse Catherine Barkley, deserts the Italian army after escaping the battle police during the retreat from Caporetto. He rows with Catherine to Switzerland, where she dies after giving birth to a stillborn son, and the novel ends with him walking back to the hotel in the rain. A frequently mocked priest also befriends Frederic.

**The Sun Also Rises**
Hemingway's 1926 novel about American and British expatriates who travel from Paris to the bullfights at Pamplona. The narrator Jake Barnes, left impotent by a war wound, loves Lady Brett Ashley, who has an affair with the former Princeton boxing champion Robert Cohn and then runs off with the young matador Pedro Romero. Its epigraph quotes Gertrude Stein's line "You are all a lost generation," popularizing the term "Lost Generation"; early on Jake also picks up the prostitute Georgette.

**"Hills Like White Elephants"**
A dialogue-driven short story from the collection Men Without Women, set at a Spanish railway station on the line to Madrid. "The American" tries to persuade his companion Jig to have "an operation," an abortion that is never named, while they drink beer ("dos cervezas") and Anís del Toro brought by a woman behind a bead curtain.

**Nick Adams and In Our Time**
Nick Adams is Hemingway's semi-autobiographical recurring character, appearing in many of the stories in In Our Time (1925), a collection that interleaves stories with short vignettes of war and bullfighting, and in later stories such as "The Killers," "The Battler," and "Fathers and Sons" (in which Nick remembers his youthful encounters with the Ojibwe girl Trudy, sister of Billy).

**"Indian Camp"**
A Nick Adams story in which young Nick goes with his doctor father to an Indian camp, where his father delivers a baby by Caesarean section with a jackknife and no anesthetic. Afterward they discover that the woman's husband, lying in the upper bunk, has cut his own throat with a razor. The story ends with Nick feeling quite sure that he would never die.

**"Big Two-Hearted River"**
The two-part story that closes In Our Time. Nick Adams, back from the war, walks past the burned-out town of Seney, Michigan, camps alone, cooks beans and spaghetti, catches blackened grasshoppers in a jar as bait, and fishes for trout. The war is never mentioned, an example of Hemingway's theory of omission.

**For Whom the Bell Tolls**
Hemingway's 1940 novel set during the Spanish Civil War, drawn from his time reporting on that war. The American Robert Jordan, a Spanish instructor fighting for the Republic, is ordered to blow up a bridge with the help of a guerrilla band led by the unreliable Pablo and his strong wife Pilar. He falls in love with the young Maria; the old man Anselmo is killed when the bridge blows, and the novel ends with the wounded Jordan lying in wait to ambush the enemy.

**"The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber"**
A safari story in which Francis Macomber shames himself by fleeing a charging lion, after which his wife Margot sleeps with the British hunter Robert Wilson. Macomber regains his courage hunting buffalo, but as a buffalo charges him, Margot fires and shoots him in the back of the head, leaving it ambiguous whether it was an accident.

**"The Snows of Kilimanjaro"**
A story about the writer Harry, who is dying of gangrene in Africa because he did not treat a thorn scratch on his leg with iodine. As vultures and a hyena wait nearby, he remembers his youth, including his time in Paris, and regrets the books he never wrote; at the end his wife Helen is awakened by the hyena and finds him dead.

**"The Killers"**
A Nick Adams story set at Henry's lunch-room, where the hitmen Al and Max, who call people "bright boy," wait to kill the Swedish former boxer Ole Andreson. The counterman George sends Nick to warn Ole, who simply waits in his room for death.

**Death in the Afternoon and the iceberg theory**
Death in the Afternoon (1932) is Hemingway's nonfiction study of Spanish bullfighting, which popularized the phrase "moment of truth" in English. In it he described his "iceberg theory" (theory of omission): the dignity of movement of an iceberg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water, so a writer can omit things he knows and the reader will still feel them.

**"For sale: baby shoes, never worn"**
A six-word story often attributed to Hemingway, supposedly written on a napkin to win a bet, though the attribution is apocryphal. His other famous pieces of writing advice include writing "one true sentence," described in his Paris memoir A Moveable Feast; his works also often explore "nada," the sense of nothingness felt by sleepless men at night.

**To Have and Have Not, Islands in the Stream, and Green Hills of Africa**
Other Hemingway books. To Have and Have Not follows the Key West boat captain and smuggler Harry Morgan, who is hired to smuggle Chinese immigrants. The posthumous Islands in the Stream follows the painter Thomas Hudson on the Bahamian island of Bimini. The nonfiction Green Hills of Africa, about a safari in Tanzania, includes his talk with the Austrian Kandinsky about a "fourth and fifth dimension" of prose and his claim that all modern American literature comes from Huckleberry Finn; he wrote it while living in Key West, in a house now home to polydactyl cats. Another story, "The Gambler, the Nun, and the Radio," centers on Cayetano, recovering from a gunshot wound in a Montana hospital.
